title: Development flow: before coding through after release
body: Development is more than the moment you write code. Before coding, confirm the goal and current state; during coding, make small changes; afterward, validate, record, and release.
detail: Splitting work into before coding → during coding → validation and review → release and operation makes the next check easier to remember. Even in a small personal project, this flow makes causes easier to trace and changes easier to undo.
when_to_show: When reviewing the overall development workflow

title: Before coding: define what success means
body: Before changing code, write down what should change and what must stay the same. This gives you concrete results to use when deciding whether the change succeeded.
detail: For example, 'the button saves' may not be enough. Include the saved format, error behavior, and whether existing data is preserved so the later test criteria are clear.
when_to_show: Before adding a feature or fixing a bug

title: Before coding: reproduce the current problem
body: Before fixing a bug, check whether the same input and steps make it happen again. Reproduction lets you compare before and after under the same conditions.
detail: Record the input, execution steps, error message, and relevant version. If you change many things before you can reproduce the problem, it becomes harder to know what the original cause was.

title: Before coding: preserve a baseline
body: A baseline is the known state before a change. Record something you can compare later, such as test results, sample output, or processed record counts.
detail: Without a baseline, a changed number can be hard to classify as improvement or breakage. Keep the same input and measurement conditions so the comparison remains meaningful.
when_to_show: Before changing performance, output, or behavior

title: Before coding: inspect the impact area
body: One changed line can affect several functions or screens that use its value. Check not only the file being edited but also where its input comes from and where its result is used.
detail: Shared functions, data formats, and storage keys can have wide impact even when the diff is small. Searching uses and call relationships helps decide what regression testing is needed.
when_to_show: Before changing shared functions or data formats

title: During coding: isolate the work
body: For a larger change, work in a separate workspace or Git branch instead of mixing it directly into the known-good version. This preserves a stable reference until validation is complete.
detail: A branch creates a boundary for experiments; it does not guarantee safety by itself. Check the current branch and changed files, then test and review the diff before integration.
when_to_show: When changing several files or experimenting

title: During coding: change one small thing at a time
body: When possible, make a small change around one cause or one feature. If the result changes, it is then easier to trace which edit caused the difference.
detail: Changing several unrelated problems at once makes a later test failure harder to localize. Repeating small change → check → next change narrows failures faster.
when_to_show: During feature work and bug fixing

title: During coding: reproduce → hypothesize → inspect → change
body: Debugging is not changing random lines. Reproduce the problem, form a cause hypothesis, inspect logs or values, make a small change, and verify again with the same method.
detail: A disproved hypothesis is still useful information. Checking input, intermediate values, and output in order usually narrows the cause better than changing several pieces without observation.

title: During coding: idempotence and rerun safety
body: Idempotence means that repeating the same operation under the same conditions does not keep changing the final state unnecessarily. It is useful for safe reruns in automation and data processing.
detail: Examples include creating an existing directory without failure or avoiding appending the same row on every rerun. Not every function must be idempotent; it matters especially when an operation may be retried.
when_to_show: When building file, batch, or automation work

title: Validation: unit, integration, and smoke tests
body: A unit test checks a small behavior, an integration test checks connected parts, and a smoke test quickly checks that an application's essential path works at all.
detail: One test type rarely finds every problem. Checking the changed function, its connection to other modules, and the real screen or execution path at different scopes reduces missed errors.
when_to_show: When deciding which tests are needed after a change

title: Validation: regression testing
body: Regression testing checks whether a new change broke behavior that used to work. Its direction is different from testing only the newly added feature.
detail: After changing a shared function or data format, recheck existing paths that depend on it instead of looking only at the edited screen. Keeping a test for a previously found bug also helps prevent recurrence.
when_to_show: After bug fixes and behavior changes

title: Validation: review the actual diff
body: A diff shows the lines that actually changed between before and after. Before committing, check that only intended files changed and that code was not accidentally deleted or left behind.
detail: A small number of changed lines does not always mean small impact. Shared functions, conditions, and storage formats can change execution paths, so inspect their surrounding code and tests too.
when_to_show: Before a commit or pull request

title: Validation: CI quality gates
body: CI can automatically run selected tests and checks when code is pushed. If a required check fails, the normal rule is to understand the cause before proceeding to release.
detail: Do not delete a failing test simply because it is old. First distinguish a code defect from a justified change to the test expectation. Automation reduces the chance of forgetting the same manual check repeatedly.
when_to_show: When using GitHub Actions or other automated validation

title: Before release: leave reproducible evidence
body: For a release, keep enough information to identify which code and input passed which validation. A version or commit SHA and the key test results are common pieces of evidence.
detail: If a problem appears later, a precise code point and validation condition are more useful than remembering that it once passed. Record input versions or environment details when they can change the result.

title: Release: prepare a rollback point
body: Rollback means returning to the previous known-good state when a new version has a serious problem. Before release, know the last good version and how to restore it.
detail: Returning only the code may not be enough if the new release already changed a data format. Check whether the release changes code, configuration, data, or several of them together.

title: After release: verify real behavior
body: Do not stop at a successful deployment message. Check that an actual user path works, and briefly inspect error logs and a key screen or API result.
detail: A development environment can pass while deployment settings or caches cause a production problem. A short post-release check finds issues early and makes rollback possible before the impact grows.
